Since The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), Habermas had been arguing that reason survives in modern life only as something people do together, that is, by giving each other reasons and staying open to being moved by them, rather than by force, money or tradition.

Between Facts and Norms was that idea turned toward law and democracy directly: a state counts as legitimate only when its laws could in principle be justified to everyone bound by them, through exactly that kind of open exchange.
I'd watched that argument take root in a decades-long intellectual history.

Habermas answered my question by going back further than any of that.
He'd been raised Lutheran.
Visiting the US in the 1960s and '70s, he'd been introduced to the Quakers, and something in their small meetings had stayed with him, specifically the way they sought unity with everyone present.

When he came to describe the conditions under which people could reason together as equals, he said he heard an echo of those meetings: conditions that hold only when everyone who could be affected by a norm isn't just included but has a voice, can object, and speaks with sincerity.
In those conditions, which go far beyond mere inclusion, the only constraint left on discourse is 'the unforced force of the better argument', as he put it in Justification and Application (1993).
